endorsements.quote: Ongoing observation after implementation of AI‐assisted robotic MT is also necessary to monitor and resolve any unforeseen implications, such as differences in outcomes or access across various patient groups, especially those in the most rural regions, where back up is limited should complications occur.

unlisted_practices: Involve regulatory bodies early in the development of AI-assisted robotic thrombectomy and establish regulatory pathways from early development to clinical practice.
Correlate in vitro measurements such as contact forces with in vivo complications such as perforation, intracranial hemorrhage, dissection, and distal embolization.
Develop and independently validate the proposed safety metrics for robotic thrombectomy, such as contact forces on vessel walls and instruments.
Use progressively complex testbeds (simple, standard, complex) across in silico, in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo stages, adding realism as development approaches regulatory certification.

Use technical navigation metrics (success rate, steps, failures, handling errors, procedure time) in in silico, in vitro, and ex vivo stages and clinical outcome metrics (mTICI, perforation, hemorrhage) in in vivo stages.
Undertake developer-focused health technology assessment and health economic evaluation early in development, alongside the technology.
Consider cybersecurity and secure data transmission before full implementation of teleoperated robotic AI-assisted thrombectomy.
Share health data for AI development within an ethical framework and prioritize patient safety and informed consent.
Establish standardized billing and coding procedures to support long-term viability of AI-assisted robotic procedures.
Test AI-assisted robotic devices with a diverse array of clinically available devices during in vitro testing.

screen.reason: This is a position statement and consensus framework detailing validation environments, testbeds, and effectiveness metrics for artificial intelligence-assisted robotic thrombectomy.
